content: Support was provided wherever feasible to assist in the implementation of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist. However, the actual adoption, execution, and clinical application of the Checklist varied significantly across countries. This variability was often attributed to limited resources and the competing demands of other healthcare improvement initiatives. Engaging the target audience through scientific publications that detailed approaches to Checklist implementation proved to be a valuable strategy. To date, over 200 scientific articles related to the Checklist have been published, which has helped sustain interest and momentum over time. These reports have primarily emphasized the importance of the 18 evidence-based recommendations for preventing surgical site infections. Mandated implementation efforts often resulted in compliance that was superficial, focusing on meeting the measurement criteria rather than the intended purpose of the Checklist. Anecdotal evidence suggested that unenforced and under-resourced mandates were frequently ineffective in driving meaningful implementation and use of the Checklist. An alternative approach to large-scale implementation involved voluntary efforts. In this model, governments or other organizations championed the Checklist, investing resources to support its dissemination, adoption, and implementation. These organizations often partnered with clinical champions or facilities to facilitate the practical application of the Checklist. Examples of such partners include professional societies, hospital associations, insurance companies, and non-governmental organizations. Voluntary adoption, by its nature, exhibited significant variability in success. Effective implementation required systematic efforts to raise awareness, convince local champions to adopt the Checklist, and provide ongoing support and resources throughout the implementation process. Large-scale mandated efforts often included active dissemination through awareness campaigns and meetings, with local champions playing a pivotal role in successful implementation. Performance measurement methods ranged from self-reporting to direct observations and audits. Modifying the Checklist to suit local needs and culture was found to enhance clinician engagement, foster a sense of ownership, and address specific local requirements. Even minor modifications, such as reviewing and adapting each item to fit the local environment, increased the likelihood of successful implementation. However, risks associated with modifications included removing beneficial items, adding excessive items that complicated execution, or altering the formatting in ways that reduced usability. Any changes needed to be evidence-based and tested in simulated environments before patient use. Voluntary implementation efforts at the national or sub-national level benefited from leveraging existing relationships to encourage participation. Visible commitments, such as signing pledges or public endorsements, were effective in engaging organizations. Leadership teams, composed of representatives from various disciplines and facility types, played a crucial role in guiding the program and promoting it across different settings. Educational efforts to support implementation were delivered through multiple channels, including webinars, in-person meetings, skills training, and coaching sessions. Webinars provided a cost-effective way to share information widely, while in-person meetings allowed participants to exchange experiences and re-energize their efforts. Skills training focused on specific clinical environments and included practical exercises to reinforce learning. Coaching visits offered direct support to local teams and provided valuable feedback to inform next steps. Monitoring progress without overburdening participating organizations was essential. Data collection needed to be streamlined and focused on providing actionable insights to support ongoing improvement efforts.
